image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #627: Tech Support Cheat Sheet

titleText.en: 'Hey Megan, it's your father. How do I print out a flowchart?'
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive title-text field is genuinely empty. The English text is the exact official xkcd image title attribute.

regions.labelEs: QUERIDOS PADRES, ABUELOS, COMPAÑEROS DE TRABAJO Y OTRAS PERSONAS "NO INFORMÁTICAS".

applications.explanationEn: Compañeros names the colleagues, and de trabajo identifies the shared workplace relationship.
Informáticas follows personas, the people it describes; no negates that description.
Informáticas uses feminine plural -as to match personas.

regions.labelEs: NO SABEMOS MÁGICAMENTE CÓMO HACER CUALQUIER COSA CON CUALQUIER PROGRAMA. CUANDO OS AYUDAMOS, NORMALMENTE HACEMOS LO SIGUIENTE:

applications.explanationEn: Mágica takes its feminine singular form and adds -mente to describe how the knowing would happen.
Cómo names the unknown method and keeps its accent; hacer stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Cualquier comes before the singular noun cosa while leaving the choice open to any one thing.
Cualquier comes before the singular noun programa while referring to any program among many.
Os identifies the several informally addressed people who receive the help, in the form used mainly in Spain.
Normal has the same masculine and feminine form, so -mente attaches directly to make normalmente.
Neutral lo turns siguiente into a general item or procedure: what follows next.

regions.labelEs: BUSCAR UNA OPCIÓN DE MENÚ O BOTÓN QUE PAREZCA RELACIONADO CON LO QUE QUIERES HACER.

applications.explanationEn: Botón is not yet identified, so que introduces parezca in the special form used for the desired description relacionado.

applications.exampleEs: RELACIONADO CON LO QUE QUIERES HACER
applications.explanationEn: Relacionado gives the description, con introduces the related topic, and lo que quieres hacer supplies that complete topic.
Lo que introduces the unnamed activity, and quieres hacer fills in what that activity is.
No appears before encuentro because the later negative word ninguno follows the verb; together they mean that not one option can be found.
Al and azar form the fixed expression meaning that the choice is random.
He is the helper used with yo, and probado is probar's completed-action form.
Probado supplies the trying action, con introduces the chosen options, and todos stands for all of those options.
Pulsa is the positive command for one familiar listener; lo attaches to identify the control being pressed.
Lo attaches to the end of the positive command pulsa, and the written accent preserves the original stress.

regions.labelEs: BUSCAR EN GOOGLE EL NOMBRE DEL PROGRAMA JUNTO CON ALGUNAS PALABRAS RELACIONADAS CON LO QUE SE QUIERE HACER. SEGUIR LAS INSTRUCCIONES.

excludedUnits.rationale: This unchanged proper brand name is not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Junto con introduces the additional search material, and algunas palabras fills that added-item slot.
Relacionadas follows the noun palabras that it describes.
Relacionadas uses feminine plural -as to match palabras.

applications.exampleEs: RELACIONADAS CON LO QUE SE QUIERE HACER
applications.explanationEn: Relacionadas agrees with palabras, con introduces the related topic, and lo que se quiere hacer supplies that topic.
Lo que introduces the unnamed action, and se quiere hacer fills in the general action someone wants to perform.
Se leaves the person unspecified, quiere stays third-person singular, and hacer names the desired action.
Ha is the third-person helper, and funcionado is funcionar's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: ¿LLEVAS MÁS DE MEDIA HORA CON ESTO?

applications.explanationEn: Más de marks a duration being exceeded, and media hora supplies that complete duration.

applications.exampleEs: LLEVAS MÁS DE MEDIA HORA CON ESTO
applications.explanationEn: Llevas marks the elapsed time for one familiar person, más de media hora gives its length, and con esto identifies what has occupied that time.

excludedUnits.rationale: This route label remains English in the Spanish raster and is not Spanish vocabulary.
This second route label also remains English in the Spanish raster and is not Spanish vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: PEDIR AYUDA A ALGUIEN O RENDIRSE.

applications.explanationEn: Pedir supplies the requesting action, ayuda names what is requested, and a alguien identifies the person asked.
Se attaches to the unchanged -ir form rendir to make the give-up verb rendirse.

regions.labelEs: POR FAVOR, IMPRIMID ESTE DIAGRAMA DE FLUJO Y PEGADLO CERCA DE VUESTRO MONITOR. FELICIDADES: ¡AHORA SOIS EL EXPERTO INFORMÁTICO LOCAL!

applications.explanationEn: Por and favor form the fixed polite expression meaning ‘please.’
Imprimid replaces imprimir's final -r with -d to address several people informally.
The -d ending marks a positive command addressed to vosotros or vosotras, mainly in Spain.
Diagrama is the main noun, de links it to its type, and flujo identifies the process-flow kind of diagram.
Pegad is the positive command for several informal listeners, and lo attaches to identify what they should stick up.
The -d command ending addresses several people informally in the form used mainly in Spain.
Cerca de introduces the nearby reference point, and vuestro monitor supplies that complete place or thing.
Vuestro addresses several people informally and matches the one masculine singular monitor possessed.
Sois is the present form of ser for several people addressed informally, mainly in Spain.
Informático and local both follow the noun experto and describe its field and scope.
Informático is masculine singular to match experto, while local has one gender form and remains singular.

cards.answerEn: dear (addressing a mixed or all-male plural group)
cards.noteEn: At the start of a message, queridos warmly addresses the people named next. It is masculine plural because the addressed list is mixed or not limited to women.

example.en: Dear neighbors, thank you for coming.

cards.noteEn: The masculine plural can mean grandfathers specifically or grandparents as a mixed group.

example.en: My grandparents live nearby.

cards.noteEn: With de trabajo, compañeros means people who work with someone.

example.es: Mis compañeros de trabajo almuerzan aquí.
example.en: My coworkers have lunch here.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to a coworker or colleague?
cards.answerEn: Say compañero de trabajo for a man and compañera de trabajo for a woman; use the plural compañeros or compañeras de trabajo.
cards.noteEn: The person word changes for gender and number. De trabajo stays unchanged and identifies the shared workplace relationship.

example.es: Una compañera de trabajo me ayudó.
example.en: A coworker helped me.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Otras goes before a feminine plural noun. Spanish normally does not put un or una before otro or otra in this meaning.

example.en: We are looking for other answers.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: non-; not a (before a category label)
cards.noteEn: Before a noun used as a label, no can divide people or things into a negative category, much like English non-. It remains a separate written word.

example.es: La entrada para no miembros está cerrada.
example.en: The entrance for non-members is closed.

cards.noteEn: Here it describes plural feminine personas. Informático or informática can also name an IT professional.

example.es: Mis tías no son muy informáticas.
example.en: My aunts are not very computer-savvy.

cards.noteEn: It describes an action as happening by magic or as if by magic.

example.es: La puerta no se abre mágicamente.
example.en: The door does not open magically.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

example.en: Lucía answers clearly.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what, how, or where to do something without naming a new person who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use an accented question word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This compact pattern is used when the person who would perform the action is already clear from context. The question word keeps its written accent even inside a larger statement: qué hacer, cómo llegar, dónde aparcar.

example.en: I do not know where to park.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “any” before one singular thing?
cards.answerEn: Put cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier libro, cualquier opción.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as libro or opción. Before a noun, cualquiera shortens to cualquier. The noun stays singular even when the meaning is any one out of many. The plus sign in the Spanish prompt means “followed by.”

example.en: You can choose any seat.

cards.answerEn: to you all; you all (informal plural, used mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Os is the short object form used with vosotros or vosotras. It identifies several informally addressed people as receiving or being affected by an action.

example.en: I am sending you all a photo.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.noteEn: Ayudamos is the present form of ayudar used with nosotros or nosotras.

example.en: We help our neighbors.

cards.noteEn: It describes what happens in the usual or expected way.

example.en: I usually arrive early.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.

example.en: The difficult part is starting.

cards.noteEn: Opción is a feminine noun, so it uses una or la.

example.en: We have another option.

cards.noteEn: It can be a physical button or an on-screen control.

example.en: Press the green button.

cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive after que when describing that unknown person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Spanish treats a known person differently from one you are still trying to find. Conozco a alguien que habla inglés means “I know someone who speaks English.” Busco a alguien que hable inglés uses hable because no particular person has been identified.
cards.questionEn: Which verb form do you use when you are looking for a person or thing that has not been identified—and may not exist?

example.es: Busco a alguien que hable inglés.
example.en: I am looking for someone who speaks English.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: seems; looks (special form for a sought or unidentified thing)
cards.noteEn: Parezca is a form of parecer. It is used here because the speaker is looking for an option that has not yet been identified.

example.es: Busca un icono que parezca útil.
example.en: Look for an icon that seems useful.

cards.noteEn: Relacionado normally uses con before the other topic or thing.

example.es: El problema está relacionado con la red.
example.en: The problem is related to the network.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one topic or thing is related to another?
cards.answerEn: Use relacionado, relacionada, relacionados, or relacionadas to match the first thing, then con before the related topic.
cards.noteEn: Only relacionado changes for gender and number. Con stays unchanged; English commonly uses ‘related to’ rather than ‘related with.’

example.es: La pregunta está relacionada con el examen.
example.en: The question is related to the exam.

cards.answerEn: to; with (required after relacionado or relacionada)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses relacionado con where English usually says ‘related to.’

example.es: La noticia está relacionada con el clima.
example.en: The news is related to the climate.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: This is the present form of encontrar used with yo. It means locating something here, not considering it a certain way.

example.en: I cannot find my keys.

cards.noteEn: Ninguno can stand alone for an understood masculine item. After a negative verb, English often uses ‘any.’

example.en: I cannot find any of them.

cards.noteEn: This is the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ir.

example.en: You can choose an option.

cards.noteEn: Uno can stand in for a masculine singular noun that has already been mentioned or is obvious from the situation, just as English can use ‘one.’

example.en: I need a pencil; give me one.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins al azar, ‘at random’
cards.noteEn: Al is normally the combined form of a and el. In the fixed expression al azar, the two words work together to mean that no deliberate choice or pattern is used.

example.en: She took a card at random.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a choice or action is made at random?
cards.answerEn: Use al azar after the choice or action.
cards.noteEn: Al azar is a fixed expression meaning that no deliberate pattern determines the result. Al is the combined form of a and el, while azar means chance or randomness.

example.en: They chose a number at random.

cards.noteEn: Azar is chance or randomness. The fixed expression al azar describes a choice or action made without a deliberate pattern.

example.en: She took a card at random.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Probado is probar's completed-action form. After a form of haber, it asks or states whether an option has been tried.

example.en: Have you all tried another solution?

cards.promptEs: probar con + persona, cosa u opción
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you will try a particular person, thing, or option to see whether it works?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of probar, then con, then the person, thing, or option being tried.
cards.noteEn: Probar by itself can mean to try, test, or taste. Con introduces the chosen possibility in this pattern. Only probar changes for the person and time; con stays unchanged.

example.en: Let's try another key.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the person, thing, or option tried after probar
cards.noteEn: In probar con, con marks the chosen possibility that someone will try to see whether it works. English normally says “try” directly before that option, without a separate word for con.

example.en: Let's try another plan.

cards.answerEn: all of them (masculine or mixed plural)
cards.noteEn: Here todos stands alone for all the previously understood options.

example.en: I have tried all of them.

cards.answerEn: press it; click it (informal singular command)
cards.noteEn: Pulsa tells one familiar person to press or click. Lo means ‘it’ and attaches at the end; the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: If you see the button, press it.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.en: Open the window.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

example.en: Sit down here!

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: Junto con introduces an additional person or thing included with the first one.

example.es: Escribe el nombre junto con la fecha.
example.en: Write the name together with the date.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is included together with another item?
cards.answerEn: Use junto con, followed by the additional person or thing.
cards.noteEn: Junto con stays together as a connector. It can often be translated as ‘together with’ or simply ‘along with.’

example.es: Mandó el informe junto con las fotos.
example.en: She sent the report along with the photos.

cards.noteEn: Con remains unchanged in the expression junto con.

example.es: Envió la carta junto con una foto.
example.en: She sent the letter together with a photo.

cards.noteEn: The -as ending matches a feminine plural noun such as palabras.

example.es: Son preguntas relacionadas con el trabajo.
example.en: They are questions related to work.

cards.answerEn: people; one; you in general (impersonal marker)
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person singular verb, se can leave the people doing the action unspecified.

example.en: People work a lot here.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona singular (persona no especificada)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish describe what people in general, an unspecified person, or ‘you’ generally do?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person singular verb and leave the person unspecified.
cards.noteEn: This impersonal pattern focuses on the action rather than naming who performs it: aquí se trabaja means ‘people work here.’ It is distinct from the reflexive use in which someone acts on themself.

example.es: En esta biblioteca se estudia en silencio.
example.en: People study quietly in this library.

cards.answerEn: one wants; people want (after impersonal se)
cards.noteEn: Quiere is third-person singular because impersonal se leaves the person unspecified.

example.es: Cuando se quiere aprender, hay que practicar.
example.en: When one wants to learn, one has to practice.

cards.noteEn: This feminine plural noun refers to steps that tell someone what to do.

example.es: Sigue las instrucciones de la pantalla.
example.en: Follow the instructions on the screen.

cards.noteEn: Funcionado is the completed-action form of funcionar and follows a form of haber.

example.en: The plan has worked.

cards.answerEn: you have spent; you have been at (for a duration)
cards.noteEn: With a span of time, llevas says how long one familiar person has already spent on something.

example.es: Llevas una hora con ese informe.
example.en: You have been working on that report for an hour.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long someone has already spent working on or dealing with something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of llevar, state the duration, then use con before the activity or thing occupying that time.
cards.noteEn: Llevar changes for the person: llevo, llevas, lleva, and so on. The duration states the elapsed time, while con introduces what has occupied it.

example.es: Llevamos dos horas con esta tarea.
example.en: We have been working on this task for two hours.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an amount is more than a particular number or quantity?
cards.answerEn: Put más de directly before the number or amount.
cards.noteEn: Use más de when the next element is a quantity being exceeded. Use más que instead when directly comparing people, things, qualities, or actions: más de diez libros, but Ana lee más que Luis.

example.en: She bought more than three books.

cards.noteEn: Before a number or other quantity, Spanish uses más de for “more than.” This de is different from más que, which commonly compares one person, thing, or action with another.

example.en: There are more than twenty people.

cards.noteEn: Media agrees with the feminine noun hora. Medio is used before a masculine noun.

example.en: I waited half an hour.

cards.noteEn: Hora can name a length of sixty minutes as well as a clock time. A number before it makes the measured duration clear.

example.en: We waited for two hours.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cards.noteEn: At a restaurant, pedir is the ordinary verb for ordering food or drink. The same verb can mean asking for or requesting something elsewhere.

example.en: I am going to order the soup.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone asks another person for help?
cards.answerEn: Use pedir ayuda, then a before the person being asked.
cards.noteEn: Pedir changes for the person and time. Ayuda stays singular in this expression, and a introduces the person asked for help.

example.es: Voy a pedir ayuda a mi vecina.
example.en: I am going to ask my neighbor for help.

cards.noteEn: Rendir becomes rendirse in this meaning. The short marker se attaches to the dictionary form.

example.en: He does not want to give up.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.noteEn: Standing alone, ¡hecho! announces that a task is complete. This differs from hecho after haber in he hecho, ‘I have done.’

example.en: Done! You can rest now.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por favor (“please”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “please”?
cards.noteEn: Por favor makes a request more polite. It can appear before or after the request.

example.en: Close the door, please.

cards.answerEn: print (positive command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Replace imprimir's final -r with -d to make the vosotros command.

example.en: Print the form.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para vosotros: hablad, comed, escribid
cards.questionEn: How do you tell several people informally to do something in Spain?
cards.answerEn: For most verbs, remove the final -r from the verb's dictionary form and add -d: hablar becomes hablad.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This positive command is used with vosotros or vosotras, mainly in Spain. If a short object word such as me is included, attach it to the end: ayudad + me becomes ayudadme.

example.en: Open your books.

cards.noteEn: Diagrama is masculine despite its -a ending: el diagrama. Many Spanish nouns ending in -ma and derived from Greek follow this pattern.

example.en: The diagram shows three steps.

cards.questionEn: What is the Spanish term for a flowchart or flow diagram?
cards.answerEn: Say diagrama de flujo; use diagramas de flujo for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Diagrama is masculine: el diagrama de flujo and los diagramas de flujo. Spanish uses de between the main noun and flujo, while English usually combines the idea into ‘flowchart.’

example.es: Dibujamos un diagrama de flujo sencillo.
example.en: We drew a simple flowchart.

cards.noteEn: Flujo can describe movement through a process. In diagrama de flujo, it refers to the routes that connect steps and decisions; this is broader than a stream of data or one program's control flow.

example.es: El diagrama muestra el flujo del trabajo.
example.en: The diagram shows the workflow.

cards.answerEn: stick it; attach it (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Pegad is the vosotros command of pegar. Lo means ‘it’ and attaches to the end.

example.en: Stick it on the wall.

cards.promptEs: cerca de + persona, lugar o cosa
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is near a person, place, or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use cerca de, followed by the nearby person, place, or thing.
cards.noteEn: Cerca is followed by de in this pattern. When el follows, de + el contracts to del: cerca del parque.

example.en: We live near the station.

cards.noteEn: Cerca normally uses de before the nearby person, place, or thing.

example.es: La estación está cerca de casa.
example.en: The station is near home.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before a masculine singular noun)

cards.noteEn: Monitor is masculine: el monitor.

example.en: The monitor is on.

cards.noteEn: Use ¡felicidades! to congratulate someone on good news or an achievement.

example.en: Congratulations on the prize!

cards.answerEn: you all are (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Sois is the present form of ser used with vosotros or vosotras, the informal way to address several people in Spain.

example.en: You all are very kind.

cards.noteEn: Here informático describes an expert's technical field. As a noun, informático can also mean a male IT professional.

example.en: We need IT support.
